newsitem.title: USA: California approves $351 million phone surcharge.
newsitem.headline: California approves $351 million phone surcharge.

text.p: California regulators said they approved a $351 million annual surcharge on telephone bills to subsidize the high cost of providing service to customers in rural areas.
The $351 million surcharge falls short of the $1.7 billion annual surcharge requested by Pacific Bell, a unit of Pacific Telesis Group, according to news reports.

The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) approved the surcharge on Friday to ensure that affordable residential basic phone service remains available everywhere in California's new, competitive telecommunications market.
For the first time, Pacific Bell, GTE California and other companies which choose to serve high-cost rural areas will be subsidized by a separate fund totaling $351 million, the CPUC said.

The funding for this subsidy will come from a surcharge on every telecommunications bill in the state of about 2.87 percent, the CPUC said. If a customer has a $35 per month phone bill for calls within the state, he or she would pay about $1 into this fund, it said.

The commission also approved a $50 million annual surcharge to subsidize telephone service to schools, libraries, hospitals and community organizations that provide education, job training or health care.
Schools and libraries will receive a 50 percent discount off the best rate they can negotiate from competing telecommunications providers.

The subsidy will come from the $50 million California Teleconnect Fund, financed by a surcharge on every telecommunications bill of 0.41 percent which amounts to about 14 cents per month on a $35 bill, the CPUC said.

Under the old monopoly-provided local phone service, rates were averaged and some services priced above cost to keep basic services affordable even in mountain and rural areas where the costs of providing service are higher.
With many companies competing to serve the same customers in a new competitive framework, these ways of subsidizing universal service are no longer feasible, the CPUC said.
It said small local telephone companies will continue to be subsidized by the existing California High Cost Fund.
Pacific Bell said the commission's plan fell short of establishing the funding needed to maintain the goal of affordable telephone service for everyone.

Pacific Bell Regulatory Vice President Rex Mitchell said the new universal service fund was an improvement over recent proposals, but did not totally replace the subsidy amount that the company's customers pay today through higher prices on some services.
"So Pacific Bell's customers are still left shouldering an additional financial responsibility that no one else will pay, which is unfair," he said.
